Fixed-dose combinations changed HIV treatment in low- and middle-income countries. Malaria still causes hundreds of thousands of deaths every year, most of them among young children in sub-Saharan Africa. Artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs) are the WHO-recommended first-line treatment for uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria, and much of the global supply is procured through public tenders and donor programmes. Artemether-lumefantrine is the most widely used ACT. It pairs a fast-acting artemisinin derivative with a long-acting partner drug, so the parasite load drops quickly and the residual parasites are cleared over the following days. t: CTD, eCTD and ACTD: a short guide to dossier formats
x: The Common Technical Document (CTD) is the internationally agreed structure for a medicine's marketing authorisation dossier, organised in five modules. The eCTD is its electronic form and is mandatory for most submissions in the US and EU. The ASEAN Common Technical Dossier (ACTD) is a regional variant organised in four parts. A generic product's dossier usually needs to be adapted to the format of each destination market.

t: CTD, eCTD and ACTD: a short guide to dossier formats: Why dossier format matters
x: When a partner licenses a generic product, the dossier is the asset that changes hands. It contains the evidence that the product is made consistently, meets its specification and is equivalent to the reference medicine. If the dossier is not in the format the destination regulator expects, it has to be restructured before filing, which takes time and money. Knowing which format a dossier is in, and which format the destination market requires, is therefore one of the first questions in any licensing discussion.

t: CTD, eCTD and ACTD: a short guide to dossier formats: The Common Technical Document
x: The CTD was agreed through the International Council for Harmonisation (ICH) under guideline M4 in November 2000. It became the mandatory format in the European Union and Japan in July 2003 and is the format the US FDA expects. Many other regulators, and the WHO Prequalification programme, use it as well. The CTD is organised in five modules. Module 1 holds regional administrative information, such as application forms and product labelling, and is not harmonised. Module 2 contains summaries and overviews, including the quality overall summary. Module 3 holds the quality data: manufacture, specifications, analytical methods and stability. Module 4 contains non-clinical study reports and Module 5 the clinical study reports. For a generic medicine, Module 4 is usually replaced by references to published literature, and Module 5 centres on the bioequivalence study against the reference product.

t: CTD, eCTD and ACTD: a short guide to dossier formats: The electronic CTD (eCTD)
x: The eCTD is the CTD delivered as a structured electronic submission, defined by ICH guideline M2. Each document sits in a defined place in a folder structure, with an XML backbone that lets the regulator track every change across the product's life cycle. The US FDA has required eCTD for new drug, abbreviated new drug and biologics licence applications since May 2017. In the EU, eCTD became mandatory in stages and now applies across procedures. A dossier held only as paper or as unstructured PDFs needs to be converted before it can be filed in these markets.

t: CTD, eCTD and ACTD: a short guide to dossier formats: The ASEAN Common Technical Dossier (ACTD)
x: Member states of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations use the ACTD, a regional format organised in four parts: Part I for administrative data and product information, Part II for quality, Part III for non-clinical and Part IV for clinical data. The ACTD's quality content is broadly aligned with the CTD, but its structure, administrative requirements and some data expectations differ. Stability data, for example, must cover the hot and humid climatic conditions of the region.

t: CTD, eCTD and ACTD: a short guide to dossier formats: What to ask a licensing partner
x: Ask in which format the dossier exists today, whether it has been filed or approved anywhere, and against which reference product the bioequivalence study was run. Ask whether stability data covers the climatic zone of your market. And ask how quickly the dossier can be adapted to your regulator's Module 1 or Part I requirements.

t: Five questions to ask before sourcing a finished dosage form: 2. What dossier exists, and in which format?
x: Ask whether the dossier is in CTD, eCTD or ACTD format, whether it is ready to file, already filed or approved somewhere, and how quickly it can be adapted to your regulator's administrative requirements. A dossier already approved by a stringent authority shortens review in many markets.

t: Five questions to ask before sourcing a finished dosage form: 3. Was bioequivalence shown against my market's reference product?
x: Each regulator names its own reference product. A bioequivalence study against the US reference listed drug may not be accepted in the EU or in other markets without additional justification or a new study. Ask which reference product was used and where the study was conducted.

t: Five questions to ask before sourcing a finished dosage form: 4. Does the stability data cover my climatic zone?
x: ICH divides the world into climatic zones, from temperate Zone I to hot and very humid Zone IVb. Stability studies must cover the conditions of the destination market, and a product's shelf life and storage statement depend on them. Ask for the zones covered and the shelf life supported.

t: Five questions to ask before sourcing a finished dosage form: 5. How will supply and changes be managed?
x: Ask how forecasts, minimum order quantities and lead times are agreed, how launch stock is planned, and how you will be notified of any manufacturing change that requires a variation to your authorisation. Good change control protects both the partner's licence and patients' continuity of treatment.
